Ruling slot 4 = Communist Party of Byelorussia under Masherov with MD sprite BLR_Communist_State (same-named successor, as done for ARM). Emigre camps: Belarusian Central Council/Astrouski (0, wartime collaborationist, US-aligned) and Rada BNR/Abramcyk (1). KGB BSSR chairman on 1 Jan 1970 is Vasily Petrov (to Aug 1970). Belorussian MD commander Ivan Tretyak (1967-76). Islamic slots use the Lipka Tatars (10, 12) and Arab student circles in Minsk (8, 9, 11). Slot 23 is an invented Grand Duchy monarchist faction (Pahonia); MD's BLR_monarchism belongs to a different, modern organization, so icon null.

0.name: Biełaruskaja Centralnaja Rada
0.text:
The Belarusian Central Council was set up in Minsk in December 1943 under German occupation as a national administration, with its own Belarusian Regional Defence militia. Its president, Radasłaŭ Astroŭski, has kept it alive in exile and, from the United States, still claims that the All-Belarusian Congress of June 1944 gave it the sole right to speak for the nation, in bitter rivalry with the Rada of the Belarusian Democratic Republic.

The council stands for an independent Belarus under a strong national authority, rid of communism and Russian domination, and seeks the patronage of Washington and the anti-communist exile front. Soviet propaganda brands its members collaborators. Its leverage lies in veterans' societies, an autocephalous Orthodox church in exile and émigré communities in America and Australia.

1.name: Rada Biełaruskaj Narodnaj Respubliki
1.english: Rada of the Belarusian Democratic Republic
1.text:
The Rada of the Belarusian Democratic Republic is the oldest government-in-exile in the world, the council that proclaimed Belarusian independence on 25 March 1918 before the Bolsheviks took Minsk. Its president, Mikoła Abramčyk, leads it from Paris, assisted by Vincent Žuk-Hryškievič in Canada, and every 25 March its supporters across the diaspora celebrate Independence Day.

The Rada stands for an independent, democratic and parliamentary Belarus within its ethnographic borders, with private property, religious freedom for Orthodox and Catholics alike and a place in the Western community of nations. It condemns both Soviet rule and the wartime collaboration of its rival, the Belarusian Central Council. Its leverage is legitimacy, the Belarusian-American Association and the sympathy of Western governments.
1.wiki: Rada of the Belarusian Democratic Republic

2.name: Hrodzienski hurtok
2.text:
The Hrodna Circle gathers the liberal Belarusian intelligentsia around the writer Vasil Bykaŭ, a frontline officer whose stark war novellas, above all The Dead Feel No Pain, printed in Novy Mir in 1966, were savaged by the party press for slandering the Soviet soldier. Bykaŭ lives in Hrodna alongside his friend Aleksiej Karpiuk, a writer and former partisan, and their readers include young poets, historians and teachers who refuse official lies.

They want honesty about the war and Stalin's crimes, freedom for the press and creative work, legality and dignity for the Belarusian language in schools and public life. They admire Tvardovsky's Novy Mir and the Moscow rights defenders and look to European humanism rather than to any bloc. Their leverage is literary prestige and readers across the Union.

3.name: Minskaja viasna
3.text:
The Minsk Spring is the reform-communist mood of Belarusian academics, editors and younger officials who hoped the Prague Spring would give socialism a human face. Its leading figure is the writer and literary scholar Aleś Adamovič, a teenage partisan who was forced out of Moscow University in 1966 for refusing to condemn the writers Sinyavsky and Daniel and now works at the Academy's Institute of Literature in Minsk.

They want democratic socialism rather than capitalism: accountable soviets, a free press, independent courts, enterprise self-management and the truth about collectivization, the purges and the war. They see Western social democrats and Italian communists as partners and detente as an opportunity. Their leverage lies in the universities, the Academy and young officials impatient with Brezhnev's caution.

4.name: Kamunistyčnaja partyja Biełarusi
4.text:
The Communist Party of Byelorussia, the republican branch of the CPSU, holds a monopoly of power in the Byelorussian SSR. Its First Secretary since 1965 is Pyotr Masherov, a former schoolteacher, partisan commander and Hero of the Soviet Union, perhaps the most popular republican leader in the Union, while Cichan Kisialioŭ heads the government. The party rules a republic rebuilt from a war that killed a quarter of its people.

Masherov pairs loyalty to Moscow with energetic modernization: tractor and truck plants in Minsk, potash at Salihorsk, oil refining at Navapolatsk and the draining of the Palesse marshes. He cultivates the partisan legend, opened the Khatyn memorial in 1969, promotes Russian as the language of progress and keeps nationalism firmly down. Its leverage is total within the republic.

5.name: Čyrvonyja partyzany
5.text:
The Red Partisans are the radical egalitarians among Belarus's war generation and the young workers of its new factories. They take their pride from the partisan republic of 1941 to 1944, when hundreds of thousands fought the occupiers in forests and marshes, and they measure today's nomenklatura, with its special shops, dachas and official cars, against the brotherhood of the brigades. No leader speaks for them openly.

They want the revolution's promise kept: equal wages, an end to privilege, elected managers, workers' councils in the Minsk tractor and automobile plants and a bureaucracy answerable to the people. Hostile to the West and contemptuous of careerists, they rely on veterans' councils, factory brigades and the partisan legend the regime itself has made into a state cult.

6.name: Žaleznaja linija
6.text:
The Iron Line is the neo-Stalinist wing of the Belarusian apparatus: district secretaries, propagandists, procurators and security veterans who never forgave Khrushchev's secret speech. They revere Stalin as the commander who liberated Belarus in 1944 and resent every rehabilitation, every bleak war story by Vasil Bykaŭ and every plea for the Belarusian language as a gift to émigré collaborators. In Moscow they look to Sergei Trapeznikov and the guardians of ideology.

They demand vigilance: purges of the writers' union, censorship of 'defeatist' war literature, harsher punishment of dissent, Russian as the sole language of advancement and Stalin's portrait back in public. Loyal to Moscow and hostile to the West, they draw on the conservatism of a war-scarred society and on party committees in the provinces.

7.name: Kamitet dziaržaŭnaj biaśpieki Biełaruskaj SSR
7.english: Committee for State Security of the Byelorussian SSR
7.text:
The Committee for State Security of the Byelorussian SSR is the republican branch of the Soviet KGB, housed on Lenin Avenue in Minsk and led since 1959 by Vasily Petrov. Heir to the NKVD that hunted nationalist and Polish underground fighters after 1944, it now watches the Polish frontier, the Catholic parishes of the Hrodna region, foreign students, émigré contacts and the small circles of national-minded intellectuals.

As a power bloc it stands for order before ideology: a sealed border, informers in every institute and factory, swift action against 'nationalist' contacts and a quiet, loyal republic. It answers to Yuri Andropov's Lubyanka as much as to Masherov. Its leverage is information, the power of arrest and files on everyone of importance in the republic.
7.wiki: Committee for State Security of the Byelorussian Soviet Socialist Republic

8.name: Majlis al-Husayn
8.text:
The Husayn Majlis is a mourning and study circle of Iraqi Shia students at Minsk's polytechnic and medical institutes, named after the gatherings held each Muharram to lament Imam Husayn. Its members follow Grand Ayatollah Muhsin al-Hakim of Najaf, the senior authority of the Shia world, whose 1960 ruling against communism and recent defiance of the Ba'athist regime have made him a hero to devout Iraqis abroad.

The circle seeks to keep faith alive in an atheist land: prayer, fasting, halal food and the rites of Muharram, alongside debates on how Islam can answer both Marxism and the West. Moderate and cautious, it wants clerical guidance and justice for Iraq's Shia rather than revolution. In Belarus its leverage is nil, but it links Minsk to the turmoil of Najaf.

9.name: Ansar al-Wilaya
9.text:
The Partisans of Guardianship are a small, secretive splinter of the Husayn Majlis: Iraqi Shia students in Minsk who find the senior clergy's caution too timid. Their inspiration is Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini, exiled by the Shah and teaching in Najaf since 1965, who preaches that Islam demands resistance to tyrants under the leadership of the jurists, together with the clandestine Dawa movement of Ayatollah Muhammad Baqir al-Sadr.

They want a revolutionary Islamic state governed by the jurists and the sharia, the fall of the Shah and of the Ba'athists, and an end to American and Soviet influence in Muslim lands. Avoiding Soviet officials and leftist compatriots, they pray and read in dormitory rooms. In Belarus they have no leverage; their eyes are fixed on Najaf and Qom.

10.name: Musulmanskaja abščyna Iŭja
10.text:
The Muslim Community of Iwye is the heart of Belarus's Lipka Tatars, descendants of Tatar warriors settled in the Grand Duchy of Lithuania from the fourteenth century under Grand Duke Vytautas. In the small town of Iwye near Hrodna, whose wooden mosque of 1884 still stands, Tatar families keep the faith of their ancestors, with smaller groups in Navahrudak, Slonim and Minsk, under the distant authority of the muftiate in Ufa.

Loyal, quiet and deeply rooted, the community wants only to pray, bury its dead in the old mizars, celebrate Kurban Bayram and pass on the kitabs, the Arabic-script Belarusian manuscripts of its forefathers. It accepts Soviet authority and asks for tolerance, not power. Its leverage is tiny but venerable: centuries of loyal service and the respect of Christian neighbours.

11.name: Halqat al-Khilafa
11.text:
The Caliphate Circle is a tiny secret study group of Palestinian and Jordanian students in Minsk drawn into the orbit of Hizb ut-Tahrir, the Party of Liberation founded by Taqiuddin al-Nabhani in Jerusalem in 1953. Like the party's cells across the Arab world, it meets in groups of a few trusted members, studies al-Nabhani's books on the Islamic state and hides its views from Soviet teachers and from Marxist compatriots.

Its goal is the restoration of the caliphate abolished in 1924: one Islamic state for all Muslims, ruled by the sharia, with nationalism, socialism and Western democracy rejected as unbelief. It hopes to win over army officers rather than wage terror. In Belarus it has no leverage, but its members plan to carry the call home.

12.name: Tatarskaje adradžeńnie
12.text:
The Tatar Revival is the reform-minded younger generation of Belarus's Lipka Tatars: teachers, engineers and students in Minsk, Hrodna and Navahrudak who fear that their faith will die with the old imams. They study the kitabs, copy prayers from Arabic-script manuscripts and look across the border to the Muslim Religious Union in Poland, whose Tatar communities at Bohoniki and Kruszyniany still keep their mosques and imams.

They want an organised Muslim life rather than private nostalgia: religious instruction for children, a registered community with its own imam, Islamic books in Belarusian and Russian and ties with believers abroad, all pursued legally and patiently. Respectful of Soviet authority yet convinced that Islam must renew itself, they have no political leverage beyond their families' pride in six centuries of history.

13.name: Savet Ministraŭ Biełaruskaj SSR
13.english: Council of Ministers of the Byelorussian SSR
13.native_full: Savet Ministraŭ Biełaruskaj Savieckaj Sacyjalistyčnaj Respubliki
13.text:
The Council of Ministers of the Byelorussian SSR is the republic's government, running its ministries, planning committee and industry under the party's direction. Its chairman since 1959 is Cichan Kisialioŭ, a careful veteran administrator who has presided over the transformation of a ravaged agrarian republic into a centre of machine-building, chemicals and electronics, and who works closely with Masherov.

The government's creed is the plan and the balance sheet: tractors and trucks for the whole Union, potash fertiliser, synthetic fibres, radio and computer plants, and the drainage of the Palesse marshes for farming. It prefers engineers to ideologists and quiet cooperation with the Union ministries to political battles, and stays neutral on language and culture. Its leverage is control of the economy and the respect Kisialioŭ enjoys in Moscow.

14.name: Biełaruskaja katalickaja misija
14.text:
The Belarusian Catholic Mission, run by the Marian Fathers at Marian House in London since the late 1940s, is the spiritual centre of Belarusian Catholics abroad. Its head, Bishop Česlaŭ Sipovič, appointed apostolic visitor for Belarusian Catholics of the Byzantine rite in 1960, leads it with Father Alexander Nadson, keeping alive the Belarusian Greek Catholic heritage destroyed at home, where the Latin parishes of the Hrodna region survive without a bishop.

The mission stands for faith, family and the Belarusian language as vehicles of national survival, joining Catholic social teaching to cultural patriotism. Anti-communist, it keeps its distance from both émigré political camps and from Cold War power politics, working through prayer, scholarship and publishing. Its leverage is spiritual: the loyalty of believers and access to the Vatican.

15.name: Dyrektarski korpus
15.text:
The Directors' Corps is the fraternity of general directors who run Belarus's new industrial giants: the Minsk Tractor Works, the Minsk Automobile Plant, the BelAZ heavy-truck works at Žodzina, the Navapolatsk refinery and the potash combine at Salihorsk. Mostly war veterans and engineers, they command budgets larger than many ministries and deal directly with the Union ministries in Moscow, often bypassing Minsk entirely.

They want more power for producers: freedom to set wages and bonuses, keep profits, choose suppliers and export abroad, with the state as a client rather than a commander. Pragmatic toward the West as a source of licences and machine tools, they care little for ideology. Their leverage is the weight of their plants in the Union economy and patrons throughout the planning apparatus.

16.name: Šabašniki
16.text:
The Shabashniki are the freelance building crews who roam the collective farms of Belarus and the wider Union every summer, putting up barns, schools and cowsheds for cash under private contracts the plan cannot match. Joined by kolkhoz market traders, private-plot farmers and the craftsmen of the second economy, they form a hidden world of free enterprise living in the gaps of socialism, tolerated because it delivers.

Their unspoken programme is economic freedom: legal private work, contracts honoured by courts, free prices at the market, the right to hire hands and keep their earnings, and an end to campaigns against 'unearned income'. Leaderless, they still have real leverage: without their labour and produce, many farms and towns would go without buildings and food.

17.name: Abaroncy Pušči
17.text:
The Defenders of the Pushcha are the zoologists, foresters and nature lovers who fight for Belaveža Pushcha, the last great primeval lowland forest of Europe and home of the rescued European bison. Since 1957 it has been run as a state hunting reserve where officials and foreign guests hunt deer and boar, while felling and drainage gnaw at its edges, and scientists of the Academy press for strict protection.

They also defend the Palesse marshes against the vast drainage programme launched in 1966, warning of dried rivers, peat fires and vanished wildlife. Patriots of their land rather than dissidents, they work through scientific memoranda, the nature protection society, the press and local museums. Their leverage is scientific authority, the sympathy of writers and Belarusians' pride in their forests.

18.name: Sialanskaja hramada
18.text:
The Peasant Hramada takes its name from the great Belarusian peasant movements, the Socialist Hramada founded in 1902 and the Workers' and Peasants' Hramada that mobilised western Belarus in the 1920s. Today it stands for the countryside's own socialism, embodied by Uladzimir Biedula, the celebrated chairman of the Savieckaja Biełaruś collective farm at Snoŭ near Niasviž, who has turned a war-ruined village into a showcase agro-town.

It wants the village to come first: collective farms run by their members rather than district officials, fair prices for produce, pensions and internal passports for farmers, investment in rural schools, roads and housing. Neither Moscow's centralism nor Western capitalism appeals to it. Its leverage lies in kolkhoz chairmen, rural district committees and the millions who still live on the land.

19.name: Uzvyšša
19.text:
Uzvyšša recalls the literary union of 1926 whose young communist writers led the Belarusization of the 1920s before the purges destroyed them together with the republic's national-communist leaders. Its surviving founder, the poet Uladzimir Dubouka, returned from decades of prison and exile and was rehabilitated in 1957; around his name gather writers, historians and party intellectuals who want Lenin's nationality policy restored.

They want a Belarusian Soviet republic in substance as well as name: Belarusian as the language of state, school and university, rehabilitation of the purged national communists, control over the republic's economy and an equal place in a voluntary union. Socialist and anti-imperialist, they distrust émigré nationalists and the West alike. Their leverage lies in the Academy, the Writers' Union and quiet sympathy among younger officials.

20.name: Kalinoŭcy
20.text:
Kalinoŭski's Men take their name from Kastuś Kalinoŭski, leader of the 1863 uprising in Belarus and Lithuania, hanged in Vilnius, whose call to the peasants to defend their land and language they treat as a creed. They are young teachers, students and village intellectuals, readers of Uladzimir Karatkievič's historical novels and of Mikoła Jermałovič's samizdat history portraying the Grand Duchy of Lithuania as a Belarusian state.

They want a nation reborn from below: Belarusian in every school and office, an end to Russification and to the flight of youth from the villages, history taught without imperial myths and, in time, a Belarusian state of its own. Suspicious of the Russian centre and of Western liberalism alike, they rely on folklore circles, local museums and the countryside's unspoken resentment.

21.name: Čorny Kot
21.text:
Black Cat takes its name from the Belarusian nationalist guerrillas who fought Soviet power in the forests after 1944, raised with German backing under the commander Michał Vituška and wiped out by the early 1950s. Its heirs are militant émigrés: veterans of the Belarusian Regional Defence and of the Belarusian units raised by the SS in 1944 and 1945, who keep in touch with the Ukrainian Bandera wing and the Anti-Bolshevik Bloc of Nations.

It preaches a militarised ethnic nationalism: a Belarus rid of Russian and Polish domination, ruled by a single national movement and liberated by insurrection when war comes. It despises the democratic Rada and rejects any coexistence with Moscow. Its leverage inside the republic is negligible, but Soviet propaganda uses its name to tar every Belarusian patriot.

22.name: Biełaruskaja vajskovaja akruha
22.text:
The Belorussian Military District, headquartered in Minsk, is the Soviet Army's main bastion on the western axis, holding tank armies and airborne forces on Belarusian soil behind the Northern Group of Forces in Poland. Since 1967 it has been commanded by Ivan Tretyak, an infantry officer decorated as Hero of the Soviet Union.

As a political force the command stands for readiness, discipline and the unity of the Union, seeing Belarus as the gateway of every invasion from Napoleon to Hitler. It distrusts Western influence and national particularism alike and would back any leadership that guarantees order. Its leverage is armed force, the prestige of the 1944 liberation and Marshal Grechko's support.

23.name: Pahonia
23.text:
The Pahonia, named after the mounted knight on the arms of the Grand Duchy of Lithuania, is the romantic monarchism of Belarusians who see the medieval grand duchy, with its Ruthenian chancery language and Lithuanian Statutes, as their own lost kingdom. Rooted in émigré circles and among a few historians at home, it dreams of a restored grand duchy and looks to the princely House of Radziwiłł, lords of Niasviž and Mir, whose best-known member, Prince Stanisław Radziwiłł, lives in London.

It wants a Christian monarchy above parties, reconciling Orthodox, Catholics and Tatars under one crown, oriented toward Europe and free of Russian rule. Its leverage is symbolic: heraldry, history and the castles of Niasviž and Mir standing as reminders of a vanished statehood.
